newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: FEATURE-Relaxed Bahrain lures ever more tourists.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Relaxed Bahrain lures ever more tourists.

text.p: It's the weekend in the Gulf, and the causeway linking Saudi Arabia and Bahrain is jammed bumper-to-bumper with American and Japanese cars.
As on every weekend, tourists from neighbouring Gulf Arab states are flocking to this tiny island state for a break.
The archipelago, the Gulf's main financial and banking hub, has become a regional tourism centre and hotels are mushrooming to accommodate increasing numbers of visitors.

Violent protests in recent years by the country's majority Shi'ite community demanding political and economic reforms by the Sunni-led government may have kept some away but did not stop the influx of tourists.
Government statistics show that tourism, already a key part of the national economy, is on the rise.
"Bahrain is providing incentives, services and facilities to lure global tourists," Assistant Under-Secretary for Tourism Kadem Rajab told Reuters.
He said 75 percent of tourists were from Gulf Arab states. "Of that, 60 percent come from Saudi Arabia," Rajab said.
"Our heritage is rich and our history and culture are major assets as tourist attractions," he said. "Bahrain offers good family entertainment and activities."
SOCIAL LIFE LURES TOURISTS TO BAHRAIN
Bahrain's 33 islands are flat, hot and humid, and cover an area of 669 square km (258 square miles) -- making the whole country smaller than New York City.
But its main attraction is not the weather, scenery or the historic forts listed in the official guide book.
"Bahrain has the advantage as a regional tourist centre because of its relaxed social environment, good services and communications," one economist told Reuters.
Alcohol, the forbidden fruit in Saudi Arabia, is served openly in Bahrain. Most other Gulf states have more restrictive alcohol policies.
Many Saudis, mostly women, see Bahrain as a more relaxed place. The dress code for women is less rigid and they can drive cars, which is illegal in their kingdom next door.
CAUSEWAY TRIGGERED TOURISM BOOM
Since the 25 km (16 mile) causeway between Bahrain and Saudi Arabia opened in 1986, about 20 new hotels have opened and the island's tourism sector has boomed.

Economists have said the political violence since 1994 including bombings and arson attacks could be keeping some visitors away. But Bahrain has managed to attract growing numbers of visitors and is investing heavily in the sector.

Government statistics showed 75,000 tourists crossed over the $1 billion causeway to Bahrain during a week-long holiday marking the Moslem feast of Eid al-Adha in April, up 115 percent over last year.
Trade, hotels and tourism are an important part of Bahrain's economy, accounting for about 11 percent of gross domestic product.
Rajab told a travel market conference in May that about two million visitors came to Bahrain in 1996 and spent $870 million. He gave no comparative figure.
He said Bahrain was improving facilities at seaports and airports, marketing Bahrain through exhibitions and increasing social activities and services to attract more tourists.
The government has spent millions of dollars to restore old buildings and forts, promote traditional crafts, and create more of the leisure parks so appealing to other Gulf nationals.
Officials said Bahrain boasted 58 hotels and was building about four new ones a year. Rajab said the new 12 million dinar ($32 million) Beach Plaza Hotel would be inaugurated at the end of 1997.
Work on a Saudi-Bahraini joint venture tourist site at a cost of seven million dinars would begin later this year, Rajab said. "There are more projects under study," he added.

Bahrain is also banking on tourism to provide more jobs for Bahrainis. Many jobs previously held by foreigners -- mainly from the Philippines and India -- are slowly being taken over by Bahrainis. Official figures put unemployment at two percent, but economists estimate it at between 10-15 percent.
